heading: How many tickets you can on average per day?
content:
On an average day, I'd say I get around 10 to 15 tickets, mostly P3s.
Out of those, I usually manage to resolve around 5 to 10 a day.
Communication happens through Teams, mail, and sometimes calls. As for
P1 tickets, those are rare --- maybe once every 3 months.

How many tickets you will resolve per day?

5 to 10 Tickets we will resolve per day.

What's is the frequency of P1 tickets?

3months once we will get a P1 ticket.

Tell Me About A Recently Faced Incident

Recently I handled a P3 issue --- a sales user was trying to process a
return and refund for a particular customer, but he wasn't able to find
that customer in his portal at all.

This ticket got assigned to me.

So, when I checked the customer table, that particular customer ID just
wasn't reflecting there. I went through our KEDB document and figured
out which job is responsible for populating that table.

I checked, and the job was still running, so I reached out to the DBA
team to ask why there was a delay.

They told me it was because of month-end --- they'd received a huge
volume of data, and because of the load, it might take another 2 hours
for the job to complete.

So, after 2 hours, I followed up with the DBA team again, and they
confirmed the job had finished.

I checked the table, and sure enough, the data was updated.

I let the user know to go check, got a screenshot from them, attached it
to the incident, marked it as resolved, and asked them to close the
ticket.

How Will You Handle P1 Issue

For any P1 issue, the first thing I do is start a bridge call
immediately.

A bridge call is mandatory because it helps us pull in all the required
resource teams and resolve the issue much faster.

As a production support engineer, it's our job to open that bridge and
add the right teams --- like system admin, DBA team, configuration team,
my manager, and so on.

If it's happening outside of business hours, I reach out to the on-call
support person for the respective team --- we maintain a Confluence page
that lists all the on-call contacts.

At the same time, I send out a notification --- we communicate to the
distribution lists to let everyone know a P1 has been opened.

And after that, every hour, I send an update notification to all the DLs
with the proper impact, after discussing it with the resource team.

So, this is how I handle a P1 issue.

Explain One P1 Issue

So, this was a P1 I handled recently. We have batch jobs that run
throughout the day they're categorized as daily, weekly, and monthly
batches.

We get alerts whenever these jobs fail or run slow, and those alerts
come through our Splunk and Dynatrace dashboards.

One night, during the night shift, we suddenly started getting multiple
alerts --- around 17 of them --- saying jobs were failing.

Since all of them were critical, I immediately opened a P1. At the same
time, I started digging into the logs by logging into the Unix server.

I found that the jobs were failing because the mount point where the
process writes its logs had gotten completely full --- 100% full --- and
that's what was causing the failures.

Since it was outside working hours, I started the bridge call right away
and pulled in the on-call support team.

I also sent out an email letting everyone know the P1 had been opened,
listed out all the impacted jobs, and after discussing with the team,
gave an ETA of 2 hours.

As an immediate fix, I worked with the Linux team to increase the space
on that mount point, so the process had enough room to write logs again.

Then I started rerunning all the failed jobs one by one --- I had to be
careful about the dependencies between them. After that, everything ran
successfully.

As a permanent fix, we configured that log mount point as a parameter in
our Splunk alerting, so now we get notified as soon as it hits 75% full,
instead of waiting until it's completely full.

After everything was sorted, I sent out an update email confirming the
issue was resolved, along with what the temporary fix was and what the
permanent fix was.

What Is Problem Management

Incident management only restore the service, it does not go to the root
cause.

When an incident keeps repeating again and again, it's not an incident,
it's a Problem.

If the incident keeps repeating itself, it loses the customer good will.

In case of the problem, the underlying issue should be fixed and the
Root Cause Analysis (RCA) has to be done.

Problem management reduces the occurrences of repeated incident.

Once we identify the RCA, we create a Jira ticket for the development
team --- could be a story or a bug --- and in that Jira, we tag the
Problem ticket along with all the incident tickets that occurred because
of this issue.

We add a proper description and attach screenshots so the dev team has
everything they need.

The development team then works on it following the standard SDLC
process --- development, SIT, and UAT --- before it goes to production.
The actual code change gets moved to production through the change
management process.

Once it's deployed, I do a health check in production to make sure
everything's working fine. If it looks good, I mark the Jira as
complete.

This is how we fix things at the root level instead of just patching
symptoms again and again.

There are different RCA techniques out there, like fishbone analysis and
the 5-why analysis --- in our company.

We specifically follow the 5-why model.

What Is Change Management

Any change cannot be done in production. we need to raise a CR (change
request). my lead will raise the Change Request Number.

All the CR request will be reviewed and approved by CAB (Change Approval
Board), This team will review these requests and ask:

• Why these changes need to be done?

• What impact will it have if we don't push this change to production?

• What is the business impact and benefits?

• They will Check all the test evidence (QA AND UAT)

The CAB call to review the CRs will happen on Wednesday (2 PM to 3PM)
and the approved CR will be moved to production on Friday/Saturday
night.

In our company we have the Change management process where we have two
releases.

- One is the weekly release

- and another is a monthly release

The change window is usually Friday evening 10 PM to Saturday morning 6
AM. During this window, all the code gets deployed, and if anything
fails, the development team jumps in to help.

As an L1 or L2, once the change is deployed, my job is to do a health
check on the application --- make sure it's up, running fine, and all
the portals are working properly. We have a checklist for this, and I go
through it manually.

.

There is check list for the application, so i need to health check-up
and manually I will check.
